screens.title: Building User Interfaces for DApps
screens.subtitle: Design frontends that surface on-chain data, accept transactions, and give clear feedback.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on building user interfaces for decentralized applications, blending standard frontend practices with the asynchronous realities of blockchain. You will learn how to display on-chain data reliably, validate and submit transactions safely, and manage a DApp’s dynamic state using React hooks. We’ll look at concrete examples: a token balance viewer that formats units for humans, a transfer form that validates addresses and amounts, and a small page that ties those components together and refreshes state after transactions. You’ll also learn the UX patterns that prevent confusing experiences—loading indicators, explicit transaction status updates, and informative error messages. By the end you’ll be able to implement interfaces that avoid common traps like stale displays, generic errors, or unnecessary gas expenditure. Think of this chapter as practical guidance: not only how to wire a contract to a component, but how to make that interaction trustworthy and transparent for end users. As you follow the examples, ask how each UI decision reduces friction and prevents costly mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: DApp UIs must clearly communicate asynchronous on-chain state, validate inputs to avoid wasted gas, and provide explicit transaction feedback so users can act with confidence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Building User Interfaces for DApps

Building User Interfaces for DApps

Practical patterns for showing on-chain data, sending transactions, and keeping the UI honest.

We’ll use React hooks and Ethers utilities for unit conversion, and we’ll emphasize loading states, validation, and clear transaction feedback. Examples include a token balance viewer and a token transfer form wired into a simple page component.

These techniques reduce user confusion and gas waste. They help you build DApps that feel responsive even when the blockchain is slow.

Explore Key Topics
Displaying Data
Fetch contract reads asynchronously, show loading, and format token units for users.
Transactions
Validate inputs, require a signer, show pending/confirmed/failed states and the tx hash.
State & UX
Manage connected account, provider, and refresh data after state-changing calls.
Coming up: code-first examples, integration into a page, and a short hands-on activity to verify your DApp on a local Hardhat node.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Live coding: balance viewer, transfer form, and integration.

Visual preview: cards show the account balance, an input form with validation, and a status line that updates after transactions. The examples use ethers.js helpers to convert between human values and wei.

In this lesson: code samples, UX patterns, and a hands-on activity to deploy and test your token DApp locally.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives will guide our work. First, you will design and implement UIs that reliably display on-chain data. That means fetching from contracts asynchronously, showing clear loading states, and formatting token units so users can read balances without confusion. Second, you will create input forms to submit transactions to smart contracts. You’ll learn to validate addresses and amounts, require a connected signer, and show meaningful transaction status. Third, you will manage DApp state using React hooks. We cover useState and useEffect for local state and re-fetching, and when to introduce context or a lightweight store for shared wallet state. Finally, you will provide clear user feedback: loading indicators, pending and confirmed messages, and parsed error messages that tell users what to do next. Each objective pairs with a verified milestone: build a token viewer, a transfer form, wire them into a page, and demonstrate a refresh after a confirmed transaction. These skills reduce frustration and prevent gas waste in real DApps.

screens.title: Skills You'll Practice
screens.subtitle: Concrete developer tasks tied to each objective

narration.text: Beyond conceptual goals, you’ll practice concrete tasks that prove competence. You’ll implement a TokenBalanceDisplay component that uses a provider and formats the raw balance with ethers. formatUnits so users see familiar numbers. You’ll build a TokenTransferForm that validates recipient addresses with ethers. isAddress, converts human amounts to wei using ethers. parseUnits, and sends a transfer transaction via a signer. You’ll wire these components into a page component that handles wallet connections and re-fetches the balance after a confirmed transfer. We will examine how to surface transaction hashes and error messages so users can inspect activity on a block explorer. You will also practice handling account and chain changes, and reactively updating the UI when the connected wallet or network changes. These tasks mirror real DApp needs and form a solid checklist for production-ready interfaces.

screens.title: Why DApp UI Needs Different Patterns
screens.subtitle: Asynchronous reads, gas costs, and trust require explicit UX

narration.text: A DApp user interface looks similar to a Web2 app at first glance, but behind the surface the interaction model is fundamentally different. Reads from the blockchain are asynchronous and can be slow; writes cost gas and require a signer. This combination means we must give users explicit state signals and avoid actions that waste gas. A clear definition: a DApp UI is a client that reads on-chain state, prompts the user to sign transactions when needed, and then updates itself when the chain state changes. Concretely, when reading a token balance you show a loading state while fetching, display the formatted balance when ready, and handle errors with helpful messages. When sending transactions you require a connected signer, validate inputs before sending, and show transaction lifecycle updates including the transaction hash so users can inspect the operation on a block explorer. A common misconception is treating transaction submission like a normal AJAX call; that can lead to poor UX and wasted gas. Instead, design flows that confirm intent, validate inputs, and surface pending status until confirmation. Think about trust and transparency: users must see enough information to know what will happen and to recover if something goes wrong. As a takeaway, a DApp UI must make asynchronous blockchain interactions visible, actionable, and reversible where possible.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DApp UIs must make asynchronous reads and gas-costing writes explicit, validating inputs and surfacing transaction lifecycle details to maintain user trust.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Why DApp UI Needs Different Patterns
Definition

A UI tuned for blockchain constraints

Reads are asynchronous and might be slow; writes cost gas and need a signer. Your UI must reflect pending work, confirm intent, and report results with clear context.

Why this matters
  • Prevent wasted gas by validating inputs before sending.
  • Reduce confusion with explicit loading and pending states.
  • Provide transaction hashes to improve traceability.
Common misconception

Treating a transaction like a normal HTTP POST leads to silent failures or expensive retries. Always await confirmation and update the UI when the on-chain state changes.

Key Takeaway

Design your DApp UI to make asynchronous and gas-impacted operations explicit and recoverable.

Analogy

Think of a blockchain write as sending a registered letter: you must prepare it correctly, pay postage (gas), and wait for confirmation that it was delivered. The UI should reflect each step.

Why this changes patterns

Because writes are costly and slow, UX must reduce mistakes and show provenance. This affects validation, feedback, and re-fetch strategies after transactions.

screens.title: Displaying On-Chain Data: TokenBalanceDisplay
screens.subtitle: Fetch balance, format units, and reveal loading and error states

narration.text: Let’s walk through a concrete balance display component. The component takes a provider, account, and token address. It uses a state for balance, symbol, isLoading, and error. On mount and whenever the provider, account, or token address changes, an effect fetches token data: the raw balance from balanceOf, the token decimals, and the symbol. The raw balance is converted to a human number using formatUnits so the user sees familiar values instead of raw wei. The component sets a loading flag while fetching so the UI can show a spinner or a loading message. It also catches errors and sets an error message that can instruct the user to retry or check their network. A practical example: the component shows "Connect wallet to see token balance" when no account is present, avoiding noisy calls. A common mistake is not handling decimal values: displaying the raw integer without formatUnits will confuse users. Another trap is re-fetching too often; use dependency arrays to re-run only when relevant inputs change. Finally, always surface errors clearly: a cryptic stack trace is less helpful than a concise message like "Failed to fetch token data: network error." Try to ask yourself: does the user understand whether data is current or stale? That question guides refresh and caching choices.

keyIdea.title: Balance pattern
keyIdea.text: Fetch balance and token metadata, convert units with ethers.formatUnits, and show loading/error states to keep the UI honest.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › TokenBalanceDisplay
Code Example
// src/components/TokenBalanceDisplay.tsx
'use client';

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { ethers } from 'ethers';
import { ERC20_ABI } from '../utils/abis';

export default function TokenBalanceDisplay({ provider, account, tokenAddress }) {
  const [balance, setBalance] = useState('0');
  const [symbol, setSymbol] = useState('');
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    async function fetchTokenData() {
      if (!provider || !account || !tokenAddress) {
        setBalance('0');
        setSymbol('');
        return;
      }
      setIsLoading(true);
      setError(null);
      try {
        const tokenContract = new ethers.Contract(tokenAddress, ERC20_ABI, provider);
        const rawBalance = await tokenContract.balanceOf(account);
        const decimals = await tokenContract.decimals();
        const formattedBalance = ethers.formatUnits(rawBalance, decimals);
        const tokenSymbol = await tokenContract.symbol();
        setBalance(formattedBalance);
        setSymbol(tokenSymbol);
      } catch (err) {
        setError(`Failed to fetch token data: ${err.message}`);
        setBalance('0');
        setSymbol('');
      } finally {
        setIsLoading(false);
      }
    }
    fetchTokenData();
  }, [provider, account, tokenAddress]);

  // Render uses conditional UI for loading/error/empty
}
Explanation
  • Use an effect to fetch balance and metadata when provider, account, or address change.
  • Convert raw units with ethers.formatUnits so values are human-readable.
  • Keep loading and error state to guide the user and avoid blank UI.
Concrete example

A user connects MetaMask, the component shows a spinner while fetching, then displays "Your CHT Balance: 123.45". If fetch fails, show "Failed to fetch token data" with a retry action in the page layer.

Key Takeaway

Always format on-chain values and make loading and errors explicit to avoid confusing raw numbers.

screens.title: Fetching Data and Managing Loading States
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach to avoid blank screens and stale data

narration.text: Fetching on-chain data requires an explicit sequence to keep the UI responsive and correct. Step one: check prerequisites. If there is no provider or account, show an explicit message like "Connect wallet" rather than attempting calls that will fail. Step two: set a loading flag and kick off the asynchronous call. This prevents flashing blank content and signals that the app is working. Step three: on success, update the relevant state fields—balances, symbols, or other contract reads—and clear the loading flag. Step four: on error, set a descriptive error message and clear loading; consider a retry affordance or advise the user to check network settings. Step five: decide when to re-fetch. Re-run the fetch when provider, account, or token address changes, and after a transaction that changes on-chain state. Avoid polling unless necessary; polling wastes resources and can produce noisy UX. A common misconception is relying solely on polling for freshness; instead prefer targeted re-fetches after confirmations. As a concrete scenario, when a transfer completes you should trigger a re-fetch of the token balance, either via a parent callback or by incrementing a refresh counter that the balance component uses as a key. This process gives users a clear and reliable picture of on-chain data while limiting unnecessary network traffic.

keyIdea.title: Fetch pattern
keyIdea.text: Check prerequisites, set loading, fetch, handle success or error, and re-fetch explicitly after state-changing transactions rather than rely on blind polling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Fetching & Loading States
Process
  1. Check prerequisites: verify provider, signer, account, and address before calling contracts.
  2. Set loading: set isLoading=true and show a spinner or message.
  3. Fetch: call contract read functions and parse results.
  4. Handle success: update state and clear loading.
  5. Handle error: set descriptive error and clear loading; surface remediation steps.
  6. Re-fetch policy: re-run on relevant input changes and after confirmed state-changing transactions.
Example flow

When the user connects, fetch balances. While fetching show "Loading balance...". If transfer completes, trigger a refresh and show the updated value.

Common mistake

Do not leave a blank area while fetching. Missing loading indicators create doubt that the app is broken. Also avoid continuous polling when a targeted re-fetch after confirmation is sufficient.

Key Takeaway

Make each fetch visible, predictable, and re-run only when necessary to keep the UI responsive and efficient.

screens.title: Input Forms and Transaction Submission
screens.subtitle: Validate inputs, require a signer, and show transaction lifecycle updates

narration.text: Now we look at building a transfer form for token transfers. The form needs local state for recipient, amount, sending flag, transaction status, and errors. Before sending, validate the recipient address with ethers. isAddress and ensure the amount parses to a positive number. If the signer is missing, show a clear message guiding the user to connect their wallet. When building the transaction, compute the amount in wei using ethers. parseUnits with the token decimals; this prevents sending the wrong value. Submit the transaction by calling transfer on the token contract connected to the signer. Immediately set a status like "Transaction sent" and include the transaction hash. Then await a receipt with tx. wait(); on confirmation, check receipt. status to determine success or failure. On success, clear inputs and trigger a balance refresh. On errors, parse common error shapes: user rejection, revert messages inside err. data. message, or generic message fields. A common pitfall is submitting without input validation, leading to revert or wasted gas. Another is failing to inform the user about wallet prompts. Always present a clear sequence: validating inputs, prompting to sign, showing pending status, and confirming or explaining failure. This structure builds trust and reduces costly mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Transaction form pattern
keyIdea.text: Validate input, require signer, parse units with ethers.parseUnits, send transfer, await receipt, and update UI on confirmation or error.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › TokenTransferForm
Code Example
// src/components/TokenTransferForm.tsx
'use client';

import { useState } from 'react';
import { ethers } from 'ethers';
import { ERC20_ABI } from '../utils/abis';

export default function TokenTransferForm({ signer, tokenAddress, onTransferSuccess }) {
  const [recipient, setRecipient] = useState('');
  const [amount, setAmount] = useState('');
  const [isSending, setIsSending] = useState(false);
  const [txStatus, setTxStatus] = useState(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  const handleTransfer = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (!signer) { setError('Wallet not connected.'); return; }
    if (!ethers.isAddress(recipient)) { setError('Invalid recipient address.'); return; }
    if (parseFloat(amount) <= 0 || isNaN(parseFloat(amount))) { setError('Amount must be positive.'); return; }

    setIsSending(true);
    setTxStatus('Sending transaction...');
    setError(null);

    try {
      const tokenContract = new ethers.Contract(tokenAddress, ERC20_ABI, signer);
      const decimals = await tokenContract.decimals();
      const amountInWei = ethers.parseUnits(amount, decimals);
      const tx = await tokenContract.transfer(recipient, amountInWei);
      setTxStatus(`Transaction sent: ${tx.hash}`);
      const receipt = await tx.wait();
      if (receipt?.status === 1) { setTxStatus(`Confirmed: ${receipt.hash}`); onTransferSuccess(); }
      else { setError(`Transaction failed: ${receipt?.hash}`); setTxStatus(null); }
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.code === 4001) setError('Transaction rejected by user.');
      else if (err.data && err.data.message) setError(`Transaction failed: ${err.data.message}`);
      else setError(`Transaction failed: ${err.message}`);
      setTxStatus(null);
    } finally { setIsSending(false); }
  };
}
Explanation
  • Validate recipient with ethers.isAddress; validate amount > 0.
  • Convert amount using ethers.parseUnits with token decimals to avoid unit mistakes.
  • Show transaction hash on send and wait for receipt to confirm success.
Concrete scenario

User enters an address and amount, MetaMask opens for signing, UI shows "Transaction sent" with the hash, and then shows "Confirmed" after a block confirmation.

Common mistake

Sending without parsing units or without checking signer often causes reverts or silent failures. Always check and convert inputs first.

screens.title: Input Validation: Save Gas, Save Confusion
screens.subtitle: Address and amount checks prevent failed transactions and wasted gas

narration.text: Input validation is a simple but high-impact part of any DApp. Before you send a transaction, validate that the recipient address is a correctly formatted Ethereum address and that the amount is a positive, non-zero number. These checks save gas and reduce user frustration. For addresses, use ethers. isAddress which performs a standardized check for address format; do not rely on regex or naive length checks. For amounts, ensure parsing with parseFloat or a numeric parser yields a number greater than zero and then convert the value to wei with ethers. parseUnits using the token's decimals. Another useful validation is ensuring the user has sufficient token balance or ETH for gas; this prevents reverts and shows a clear, actionable message like "Insufficient token balance" or "Not enough ETH for gas." A common misconception is that the wallet will always surface exact error reasons; wallets may show low-level errors, so your frontend should catch and present a clear next step. Validation also includes guarding UI inputs against malicious content—sanitize any user-provided display strings to prevent XSS when rendering comments or metadata. In short, validation guards both user funds and your app's reputation. Implementing these checks up front is cheap and prevents costly mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Validation rules
keyIdea.text: Check addresses with ethers.isAddress, ensure amounts parse to positive numbers, and verify balances before sending transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Input Validation
Checks to implement
  • ethers.isAddress(recipient) for address validity.
  • parseFloat(amount) > 0 and not NaN for amounts.
  • Convert with ethers.parseUnits(amount, decimals) before sending.
  • Verify sufficient token balance and sufficient ETH for gas.
  • Sanitize display strings to avoid XSS when showing user content.
Example error messages
Invalid recipient address. Check the address and try again.
Amount must be a positive number.
Insufficient ETH for gas. Fund your wallet or reduce gas settings.
Why it matters

Front-end validation prevents needless blockchain calls, saving users gas and time, and leads to clearer UX when something goes wrong.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle and User Feedback
screens.subtitle: Inform users at each stage: sent, pending, confirmed, failed

narration.text: Understanding the transaction lifecycle helps you design precise feedback. When a user sends a transaction, there are distinct stages. First, the wallet prompt where the user signs or rejects. If rejected, report that explicitly. Second, on send, the network returns a transaction hash and you can show "Transaction sent" and the hash so the user can follow it on a block explorer. Third, the transaction is pending: show a pending indicator and explain it may take time depending on gas and network. Fourth, wait for a confirmation by calling tx. wait(); on a successful receipt with status 1, show a confirmed message and trigger a re-fetch of related on-chain data. If receipt indicates failure, show the failure with the hash and any parsed revert reason. For exceptions during send, parse common error objects to display helpful messages such as "Transaction rejected by user" or "Insufficient funds." A common UX mistake is showing only a spinner without context or a hash to investigate. Another is assuming a single confirmation is always enough; explain how many confirmations your DApp trusts. As a practical rule, always show actionable next steps: "View on explorer", "Retry", or "Contact support with tx hash." This clear lifecycle reduces anxiety and enables users to recover when things go wrong.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle stages
keyIdea.text: Wallet prompt → Transaction sent (hash) → Pending → Confirmed or Failed; provide clear messages and next steps at each stage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Transaction Lifecycle
Stages
Wallet Prompt

User signs or rejects. If rejected, show "Transaction rejected by user."

Sent (Hash)

Show the tx hash immediately so users can inspect the pending tx.

Pending

Show a spinner and note expected wait time or confirmation count.

Confirmed / Failed

On receipt, show success with hash or failure with parsed revert reason and next steps.

Concrete example

After sending, display: "Transaction sent: 0xabc... Waiting for confirmation..." Then update to "Confirmed: 0xabc..." and refresh balances.

Key Takeaway

Provide a clear lifecycle view and actionable next steps using the transaction hash as the primary anchor.

screens.title: Managing DApp State with React Hooks
screens.subtitle: Local state vs shared wallet/provider state and re-fetch triggers

narration.text: State management in a DApp centers on wallet and contract-derived data. Use useState for local UI concerns: form inputs, isLoading flags, txStatus, and small component-specific state. Use useEffect for side effects such as fetching on-chain data when dependencies change—provider, account, tokenAddress, or a refresh trigger. For shared state that many components need—connected account, provider, signer—use context or a lightweight global store. This avoids prop drilling and ensures a single source of truth for wallet state. A useful pattern is to expose a refreshBalanceTrigger or incrementing key from the top-level component; child components include that key in their dependencies so they re-fetch when a transaction completes. Also handle wallet events like accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect to reset state and reinitialize the provider and signer. A common misconception is to keep everything local: that can lead to inconsistent state across components. Another trap is overusing polling. Prefer event-driven re-fetching after a confirmed transaction. Concretely, when a transfer confirms, call the parent callback handleTransferSuccess which increments a refresh counter used as a key on TokenBalanceDisplay. This approach keeps the UI synchronized without unnecessary network traffic and keeps component responsibilities clear.

keyIdea.title: State pattern
keyIdea.text: Use useState/useEffect for local state, context or store for wallet/provider, and an explicit refresh trigger to re-fetch after transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Managing DApp State
Architecture

Top-level app holds provider, signer, account, and a refresh trigger. Child components receive provider/account or use context. TokenBalanceDisplay uses provider, account, tokenAddress, and a key based on the refresh trigger to re-fetch after transactions. TokenTransferForm calls onTransferSuccess to increment the trigger in the parent.

Local state

Form inputs, loading flags, errors.

Shared state

Provider, signer, connected account stored in context or a global store.

Event handling

Listen to accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect to update state and inform the user when reconnection is needed.

Key Takeaway

Separate local and shared concerns, and use an explicit refresh trigger to synchronize reads after writes.

screens.title: Integrating Components into a Page
screens.subtitle: Connect wallet, pass provider/signer, and refresh after transfers

narration.text: Integration ties the components together into a cohesive DApp flow. The page component manages connecting the wallet, storing provider, signer, account, and a refresh balance trigger. It registers event listeners for accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect to keep the UI in sync. When the wallet connects successfully, read the network and update a status message. Render TokenBalanceDisplay and TokenTransferForm only when an account is present to avoid unnecessary errors. Provide an onTransferSuccess callback that increments a refresh trigger so the balance component re-fetches. The page uses keys or dependency arrays so children re-run effects when the trigger changes. A concrete scenario: user clicks Connect Wallet, the page initializes a BrowserProvider and signer, and TokenBalanceDisplay fetches the balance. The user submits a transfer; TokenTransferForm sends the tx and on confirmation calls onTransferSuccess which increments the trigger. TokenBalanceDisplay then re-fetches and shows the updated balance. A common mistake is not handling network mismatches—show the user when they are on an unsupported chain and explain how to switch. By centralizing wallet state and refresh logic in the page, components stay focused on presentation and behavior without duplicating connection logic.

keyIdea.title: Integration pattern
keyIdea.text: Keep wallet connection logic at the page level, render components conditionally, and use a refresh callback to synchronize state after transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Integrating Components
Example Snippet
// src/app/page.tsx (excerpt)
'use client';

import { useEffect, useState, useCallback } from 'react';
import TokenBalanceDisplay from './components/TokenBalanceDisplay';
import TokenTransferForm from './components/TokenTransferForm';

export default function Home() {
  const [account, setAccount] = useState(null);
  const [provider, setProvider] = useState(null);
  const [signer, setSigner] = useState(null);
  const [refreshBalanceTrigger, setRefreshBalanceTrigger] = useState(0);

  const handleTransferSuccess = useCallback(() => {
    setRefreshBalanceTrigger(prev => prev + 1);
  }, []);

  return (
    // Render status, connect wallet control, and conditionally show balance and form
    // TokenBalanceDisplay key={refreshBalanceTrigger} will re-fetch when trigger changes
  );
}
Explanation

Centralize connect logic and event listeners at the page level. Pass provider and signer down as props or through context. Use a numeric trigger to force child re-fetches after confirmation.

Concrete scenario

After a confirmed transfer, call handleTransferSuccess to increment refreshBalanceTrigger. TokenBalanceDisplay includes that trigger in its dependency array and refetches balance.

Key Takeaway

Keep connection and refresh logic in one place so components remain simple and reactive.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid these pitfalls: stale UI, poor error parsing, and XSS

narration.text: This lesson lists frequent mistakes and how to avoid them. Mistake one: ignoring loading states. If you do not show a loading indicator, users assume the app is broken. The fix is explicit isLoading flags and concise messages. Mistake two: poor error handling. Generic errors that say "something went wrong" leave users helpless. Instead, parse known error shapes from Web3 libraries to give actionable feedback, such as "Transaction rejected by user" or "Insufficient funds." Mistake three: lack of input validation that sends malformed transactions and wastes gas. Validate address format and amounts before calling the chain. Mistake four: not refreshing on confirmed transactions, leaving stale displays. Trigger re-fetches on confirmation or rely on events where available. Mistake five: XSS risks when displaying user-generated metadata; sanitize content before rendering. Mistake six: blind gas estimation overrides. Never auto-resubmit with higher gas without explicit consent. Applying these fixes improves reliability and trust: users see meaningful feedback, avoid preventable costs, and have a clear path to resolve issues. As a practical tip, log error details to the console for debugging but present a friendly, actionable message to the user. This balance keeps developers informed while protecting user experience.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls to avoid
keyIdea.text: Show loading, parse and present errors, validate inputs, refresh after confirmation, sanitize content, and avoid automatic gas resubmits.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Common Mistakes
Ignoring loading

Show spinners or messages during async reads to avoid blank screens.

Generic errors

Parse library errors and give actionable guidance rather than "something went wrong."

No validation

Validate addresses and amounts before sending to save gas and time.

Stale UI

Re-fetch after confirmed transactions rather than relying on manual refresh.

XSS risks

Sanitize any user content before rendering to avoid cross-site scripting.

Gas estimation

Do not auto-resubmit with higher gas without consent; explain options to the user.

Pro tip

Log detailed errors for debugging but surface concise, actionable messages for users to keep the experience clear and safe.

screens.title: Activity: Build a Token Viewer and Transfer DApp
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step checklist to implement, deploy, and verify on a local Hardhat node

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties everything together. Begin with a Next. js project and ensure your Hardhat node is running. Deploy a simple ERC-20 token contract such as the provided MyToken contract and copy its deployed address. Add the ERC-20 ABI to src/utils/abis and import it into your components. Implement TokenBalanceDisplay using a provider and useEffect to fetch balance, decimals, and symbol. Implement TokenTransferForm with recipient and amount inputs, validate them with ethers. isAddress and parseFloat, and convert amounts with ethers. parseUnits. In src/app/page. tsx centralize wallet connection: set provider, signer, and account state; listen to accountsChanged and chainChanged; and add a refreshBalanceTrigger to force re-fetches. Pass onTransferSuccess to TokenTransferForm to increment the trigger when a transfer confirms so the balance re-fetches. Run the app, connect MetaMask to your local Hardhat network, and test transferring tokens between accounts from the node output. Verify the balance updates after confirmation. screens.title: Optimistic Updates vs Re-fetch on Confirmation
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between instant UI updates and accurate on-chain state

narration.text: When a user initiates a state-changing transaction you have two main UX approaches: optimistic updates or wait-for-confirmation re-fetch. Optimistic updates immediately reflect the expected result in the UI before the transaction confirms. This makes the app feel instant, but it risks showing incorrect state if the transaction fails or is reverted. If you use optimistic updates, provide a clear rollback strategy: show the pending transaction and allow undoing or re-syncing if the transaction fails. Re-fetch on confirmation waits for a receipt before updating the UI, which is accurate but can feel slow. For many token transfers, the recommended compromise is to show an immediate status change that is explicitly labeled as "pending" and to optimistically update a transient display while still keeping the authoritative balance tied to confirmed data. After confirmation, refresh the canonical state. Common misconception: optimistic updates eliminate the need for confirmations. They do not; they only improve perceived responsiveness and must be paired with explicit pending indicators and reconciliation logic. Choose the pattern based on risk tolerance: critical financial flows favor confirmed re-fetches; less risky UX flows can employ optimistic display with reconciliation. Always show the transaction hash so users can inspect the real state on a block explorer.

keyIdea.title: Pattern choice
keyIdea.text: Use optimistic updates for perceived speed with clear pending labels and rollback plans; prefer confirmed re-fetches for critical or high-risk flows.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Optimistic vs Confirmed
Optimistic Update

Immediately reflect expected changes and label them as pending. Provide rollback or re-sync if the transaction fails.

- Pros: faster perceived UX.
- Cons: risk of showing incorrect state until confirmed.
Re-fetch on Confirmation

Wait for tx.wait(), then re-fetch authoritative on-chain data before updating canonical UI values.

- Pros: accurate state, fewer reconciliation issues.
- Cons: slower user feedback.
Practical compromise

Use optimistic updates only with explicit pending labels and always confirm with a re-fetch after receipt. Provide the transaction hash so users can independently verify status.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to carry forward

narration.text: These three concise concepts summarize the chapter. First, UI/UX matters: users need clear, honest states for asynchronous reads and gas-costing writes. Second, validation and unit conversion are essential: check addresses and amounts before sending and convert between human values and wei using ethers. formatUnits and ethers. parseUnits. Third, explicit transaction feedback and state synchronization reduce confusion: show pending and confirmed states, include transaction hashes, and re-fetch after confirmed transactions to keep the UI authoritative. Keep these principles in mind as you build DApps: they prevent wasted gas, improve trust, and make interfaces maintainable.
